html:
Neo-Confucianism is the revived form of Confucian thought that took shape in China under the Song dynasty in the 11th and 12th centuries, and became the ruling philosophy of China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for centuries.

Song scholars wanted to answer Buddhism and Daoism, which offered deep accounts of the mind and the universe, with something just as deep from the teaching of Confucius and Mencius. They taught that all things are made of qi, vital matter, shaped by li, principle. To become a good person one studies the principle in things and in oneself, and cultivates the mind.

  • Zhu Xi pulled these ideas together in the 1100s. His commentaries on the Four Books became the basis of the imperial examinations from 1313 until 1905.
  • Wang Yangming of the Ming dynasty taught instead that principle lies in the mind itself, and that knowing and acting are one.

In Korea the Joseon dynasty made it the state teaching. Its law code, the Gyeongguk daejeon, rested on its ideas, and Yi Hwang became its greatest Korean thinker. In Japan the Tokugawa shoguns backed Zhu Xi's school. Everywhere it stressed duty to parents and rulers, family ritual and a fixed social order, and it was blamed in the 1800s and 1900s for holding back change.
sum: Neo-Confucianism is the revived form of Confucian thought that took shape in China under the Song dynasty in the 11th and 12th centuries, and became the ruling philosophy of China, Korea, Japan and Vietnam for centuries.
